tagline.steam: Valve's store, from Steam's content servers
tagline.epicgames: The Epic Games Store, from Epic's CDN

blizzard.cdn: Content comes from Blizzard's CDN hosts under /tpr/<product>/; the product code names the game (osi is Diablo II: Resurrected, hs is Hearthstone).
blizzard.launcherData: Catalogs, configs and the bnt directories are the launcher's own data: its list of products, their build configurations, the launcher and its bootstrapper.
blizzard.builds: Each game's current build is checked with Blizzard's patch service every few minutes; a game is current when the stash holds all of that build's install (the files its download manifest lists for Windows, the configured locale and region), and a percentage says how much of it the stash holds. A pre-release build, which the launcher downloads ahead of a launch, shows up when Blizzard publishes one.
blizzard.ranges: Large archives are fetched in ranges, so a game is often only partly in the cache.
blizzard.art: Key art and icons come from the launcher's own product catalog, which lanstash reads from Blizzard's CDN once and keeps.

steam.depots: A game arrives as depots (its content split by platform and language), each stored on its own; the depots of one app are shown together, under the app's store art.
steam.crc: Chunks are checked against the CRC Steam sends with them before they are kept.

epicgames.directories: A game's downloads are filed under a directory of their own, not its app id; lanstash shows them under the app, with its name and art.
epicgames.sha: Chunks from Epic's CDN are checked against the SHA-1 their build's manifest gives before they are kept.
epicgames.oldBuilds: Old builds' segments go on their own once the current build is held whole and a week passed unused; Prune on a game's page shows what would go.

windows.label: Set up Epic Games on Windows

download.title: Download it and start it once
download.made: Made by lanstash for this network
download.text: The first time, Windows may ask whether to run a downloaded file: Run. It puts itself in place and makes an "{{shortcut}}" shortcut on the desktop and in the Start menu; pin either.

shortcut.title: Start Epic with that shortcut from now on
shortcut.text: In place of Epic's own shortcut: it sets Epic up, then starts it, each time.

runs.title: What it does, each start
runs.label: What the shortcut runs, and as whom
runs.close: Closes the Epic launcher, if it is running.
runs.add: Adds these lines to Epic's settings file:
runs.admin: Only where Windows refuses that: Windows asks you first, then the same lines are added, and nothing else.
runs.start: Starts the launcher as it always starts: never from the administrator's session.

check.title: Check that it works
check.text: Install or update any game. It shows under Activity while it downloads and under Cached once it is done. If it shows in neither, the launcher is still downloading over HTTPS.
